lead: A gear tooth does not see one fixed load all its life. It sees a load spectrum: full load for some hours, part load for others, a shock at each start. The tooth collects fatigue damage cycle by cycle, so gear life design turns the spectrum into one equivalent load, sizes the gears for it, and then checks the rest of the gearbox: ratio split, shafts, bearings, heat and lubrication. The same method sizes the reducer of a textile mill, a crane hoist or an electric-vehicle drive.
prereq: You need: the S-N curve and endurance limit from fatigue design, and the checks of spur gear design.

blocks.text: Gear life is counted in load cycles on one tooth. A gear turning at n rpm for Lh hours meets the load N = 60 n Lh times; a gear at 1200 rpm for 8000 h sees 5.76 × 10⁸ cycles. Because the pinion turns faster, its teeth collect more cycles than the gear's, which is the reason for the harder pinion in gear materials.

The S-N curve plots the alternating stress against the cycles to failure. On log-log axes it falls as a straight line, which can be written F<sup>k</sup> N = constant for a load F, with k the life exponent; for many steels it flattens at the endurance limit. Bending fatigue starts at the root fillet and contact fatigue (pitting) at the flank, so each has its own curve and exponent. For contact the load-life exponent is often taken as 3, because the contact stress grows only with the square root of the load.

Miner's rule adds the damage of each load level: D = Σ ni/Ni, where ni is the number of cycles spent at level i and Ni the cycles to failure at that level from the S-N curve. Failure is predicted when D reaches 1; designers keep D below 1 for reliability.

Let a load spectrum give the power P<sub>i</sub> (or torque T<sub>i</sub>) at each duty point and the fraction p<sub>i</sub> of the life spent there, at a constant speed. Miner's rule with the life exponent k gives the steady load that does the same damage:

Peq = (Σ pi Pik)1/k Peq is the equivalent power in kW; the fractions pi add to 1; k = 3 for contact fatigue. For a torque spectrum put Ti in place of Pi. If the speed changes between duty points, use cycle fractions ni/Σni instead of time fractions.

For bending the exponent is larger, so do not reuse the contact P<sub>eq</sub> for a bending check. The design load is P<sub>design</sub> = C<sub>s</sub> P<sub>eq</sub>, where the service factor C<sub>s</sub> allows for the driver and the machine (shock, starting, reversing). Two easy mistakes go in opposite directions: the maximum load for the whole life over-sizes the gears, and the simple average under-sizes them, because damage grows with the cube of the contact load.

One stage of spur or helical gears suits ratios up to about 5 or 6; beyond that the pinion becomes too small or the gear too large. A two-stage box splits the ratio, i = i<sub>1</sub> i<sub>2</sub>. An equal split, i<sub>1</sub> = i<sub>2</sub> = √i, keeps the stages similar; many designers give the first (fast) stage a slightly larger ratio so that the two gear wheels dip equally into the oil. The second stage carries i<sub>1</sub> times the torque of the first, so its gears are larger.

The housing holds the bearing bores in line, holds the oil and passes heat to the air; ribs stiffen it. At moderate speed the larger gears dip into the oil and splash it on to the teeth and bearings; at high speed a pump sprays oil on the mesh and a cooler may be added. Seals keep oil in and dust out, and a breather stops pressure building up. In steady running the heat made equals the heat lost:

Pin (1 − η) = k A (t − t0) Pin is the input power in W, η the overall efficiency (about 0.98 per spur or helical stage), k the heat transfer coefficient in W/(m²K), A the housing area in m², t the oil temperature and t0 the air temperature.

A gearbox can fail first on bearing life, oil temperature or a leaking seal, not on its teeth, so each gets its own check; bearings are selected from their load ratings and life in the unit on bearings.

examples.question: A gearbox runs at 1000 rpm for 10 000 h. It transmits 10 kW for 60 % of the time, 6 kW for 30 % and 2 kW for 10 %. For contact fatigue take k = 3. Find the equivalent power, compare it with the maximum and the average, and find the cycles on a tooth.
steps: P<sub>eq</sub> = 665.6<sup>1/3</sup> = 8.73 kW (a cube root, not a division by 3).
Compare: the maximum is 10 kW (15 % more than P<sub>eq</sub>, so sizing on it over-sizes); the average is 0.6 × 10 + 0.3 × 6 + 0.1 × 2 = 8.0 kW (8 % less, so sizing on it under-sizes).
examples.answer: P<sub>eq</sub> = 8.73 kW against a 10 kW maximum and an 8.0 kW average; each tooth sees 6.0 × 10⁸ cycles.

examples.question: A conveyor drive takes 10 kW at 1440 rpm and needs an output of about 72 rpm through two spur stages, each 98 % efficient. Split the ratio, choose tooth numbers (pinions of 20 and 18 teeth), find the speeds and torques, and the oil temperature for a housing of 1.0 m² with k = 15 W/(m²K) in air at 35 °C.
steps: Total ratio i = 1440/72 = 20. Equal split: √20 = 4.47 per stage.
Stage 1: 20/90 gives i<sub>1</sub> = 4.5. Stage 2: 18/80 gives i<sub>2</sub> = 4.444. Overall 4.5 × 4.444 = 20.0.
Speeds: shaft 1 at 1440 rpm, shaft 2 at 1440/4.5 = 320 rpm, output 320/4.444 = 72 rpm.
Efficiency: η = 0.98 × 0.98 = 0.9604; output power 9.604 kW; heat to lose = 10 000 × 0.0396 = 396 W.
Oil temperature: t − t<sub>0</sub> = 396/(15 × 1.0) = 26.4 K, so t = 35 + 26.4 = 61.4 °C, below the usual 80 °C limit: natural cooling is enough.
examples.answer: Stages 20/90 and 18/80 (4.5 × 4.444 = 20); torques 66.3, 292.4 and 1273.8 N·m; 396 W of heat; oil at about 61 °C.

traps: Using the maximum power for the whole life over-sizes the gears; using the average under-sizes them.
Writing P<sub>eq</sub> = Σ p<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub>³ / 3. It is the cube root of the sum: (Σ p<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub>³)<sup>1/3</sup>.
Counting life in hours and forgetting the speed: N = 60 n L<sub>h</sub>, and the pinion collects more cycles than the gear.
Using the contact exponent 3 for a bending check.
Forgetting that the second stage carries more torque: size each stage with its own torque, after the losses of the stage before it.

quiz.q: What is the endurance limit of a gear material?
quiz.a: The alternating stress below which the S-N curve is flat, so the life is treated as infinite.
D = Σ n<sub>i</sub>/N<sub>i</sub>; failure is predicted when the damage sum D reaches 1.

quiz.q: Why is gear life counted in cycles rather than hours?
quiz.a: Fatigue damage depends on the number of load repetitions. Speed decides how many cycles an hour brings: N = 60 n L<sub>h</sub>.

quiz.q: A gear at 2000 rpm for 5000 h carries 8 kW for half the time and 4 kW for the other half. Take k = 3. Find P<sub>eq</sub> and the cycles.
A two-stage box has a total ratio of 16. Give an equal split and the torque on the output shaft for 5 kW at 960 rpm, each stage 98 % efficient.
A gearbox passes the tooth checks but its oil runs at 95 °C. What will you check and change?
quiz.a: Check the efficiency, the housing area, the oil level and the bearings. Raise kA with fins or a fan, add an oil cooler, or use a larger housing.

quiz.q: A crane gearbox has more heavy lifts than planned. Why does its life fall much faster than the load rises?
quiz.a: Damage grows with the load to the power k (3 for contact, more for bending), so a few more heavy cycles raise the damage sum D sharply and life falls roughly with the cube of the equivalent load.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gearbox makers rate gears to ISO 6336 or AGMA standards using measured load spectra, and model the housing as a thermal network to predict oil temperature. In service, oil analysis and vibration monitoring catch pitting before a tooth breaks. Electric-vehicle reducers add noise limits and motor torque ripple to the load spectrum. Search for gear load spectrum, gearbox thermal rating and condition monitoring of gearboxes.
